5162-agatha-webb:
Anna Katharine Green's mystery centres on a cry heard on a hill, a night's work. An empty drawer becomes full, as detective and neighbours try to understand the death of Agatha Webb. Chapters follow a purple orchid, a man with a beard. A detective named Knapp arrives, while local gossip and careful deduction pull the truth into view piece by piece.

Green builds the puzzle through objects: slippers, a flower, and the small facts a sharp observer notices. The novel shows her mature method at work, combining a village mystery with courtroom clarity. It rewards readers who like to weigh each clue before the solution arrives.
59060-the-disappearance-of-kimball-webb:
Rowland Wright wrote The Disappearance of Kimball Webb, a mystery novel copyrighted in 1919 and published at New York in 1920 by Dodd, Mead and Company. The first chapter is a mysterious disappearance, and Kimball Webb himself is said not to look the part of trouble as it opens. Henrietta telephones, Elsie suspects and makes inquiries, and an aunt's will enters the case. A haunted room and a man named Joe Allison follow.

Later chapters bring conclusions from a detective figure named Coe, an expected letter, a man in uniform, and Elsie's birthday. Wright builds a light country-house mystery of the period, with a vanished man at its centre.
62066-the-annual-report-on-the-health-of:
T Orme Dudfield, medical officer of health, wrote this annual report on the health of the parish of St Mary Abbotts, Kensington, for the year 1874. It was printed at Kensington in 1875. Such reports were the front line of Victorian public health, counting births, deaths, and diseases parish by parish.

The contents show the work in detail. Dudfield accounts for a higher death rate in 1874 and compares local and London rates. He treats measles and scarlet fever, and blames some outbreaks on contaminated milk and the milk of diseased cows. He notes too many dairies, uncertified deaths, and abuse of death certificates. Tables track marriages, births, and deaths by ward and by cause.
71624-elijah-cobb:
Elijah Cobb, 1768 to 1848, a Cape Cod skipper, is a memoir volume issued by Yale University Press in 1925. It was published on the McMillan memorial foundation at Yale in that year. Paine wrote a foreword for the book of the old captain papers. A portrait from a French pastel of 1794 fronts the volume for the reader.

He was tall and straight, of fine figure, the caption under that portrait records of Cobb. He was distinguished for his sturdy integrity as well as talent in the words of the caption. The book prints the journals and accounts of a Brewster sea captain of the early republic. Cobb traded to Europe in the years of the French wars, was taken, intrigued, and kept his books through it all. His papers are a first rate record of the small ship Yankee trade, published a century after his voyages.
agatha-webb:
Anna Katharine Green's Agatha Webb opens the morning after a dance in Sutherlandtown. A cry on the hill has been heard in the night, and the great house's guests have departed. Agatha Webb, a grand woman with a hidden past, is found murdered in her cottage. Money is missing from one drawer, and money remains untouched in another.

Detective Knapp arrives from the city, but local talent does the work. Young Sweetwater reasons and acts through the middle book, following slippers, a purple orchid, and a scrap of paper. The Zabel brothers, a sinister pair, darken the inquiry. Father and son of the Sutherland house guard the final secret. Green structures the tale in three books of rising revelation. Her small-town mystery keeps its solution locked until Sweetwater pays his debt at last.
britannica-1911-robinson-henry-crabb:
Henry Crabb Robinson was an English journalist and diarist born at Bury Saint Edmunds. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the son of a tanner into a London law office in 1796. Two years later a legacy gave him a small steady income of his own. In 1800 he set out on a long tour of Germany and Bohemia.

He entered the university of Jena in 1802 and stayed until 1805 on his return. Those German years shaped the mind that later kept famed diaries of his age. Friendships with poets and thinkers grew from that student time abroad. The entry sets up the life of a man whose journals outlast his journalism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benjamin-jose:
Benjamin Joseph Webb, a Kentucky editor and historian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Bardstown in 1814, he died at Louisville in 1897. His father was an early Kentucky pioneer and a convert, and Benjamin learned the printer's trade after leaving St. Joseph's College young.

In 1836 he took up the Catholic Advocate at Bardstown, a paper he ran with help from Bishops Spalding, David, and Flaget. Later work as a historian of Kentucky Catholic life, including a centenary history, made him the state's memory keeper. The entry sketches a newspaperman turned chronicler of his church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-banniste:
John Bannister Tabb was an American poet and teacher whose brief, polished lyrics won wide admiration. Born near Richmond in 1845 to an old Virginian family, he lost much of his sight at fourteen and turned to the piano. He then served in the Confederate navy until captured in 1864. Imprisoned at Point Lookout, he formed a lasting friendship with Sidney Lanier.

After the war he taught at St. Paul's School in Baltimore, followed his rector Alfred Curtis into the Catholic Church in 1872, and prepared for the priesthood at St. Charles's College, where he stayed to teach English until near his death, by then totally blind. His poems, collected in five volumes, give life to inanimate things and make abstractions concrete. They aim, as his own opening lyric puts it, for brevity that lingers in love and memory.
tacitus-annals-church-brodribb:
Roman historian Tacitus wrote the Annals, a cold-eyed record of emperors from Tiberius to Nero. Translators Church and Brodribb gave the work its classic English form. Tacitus served Rome at high rank and knew power from inside.

He traces courts full of fear, spies, and staged trials. Seneca, Agrippina, and Nero pass in chilling scenes. His prose is terse, dark, and full of moral sting. Whole books are lost, yet what remains defines imperial Rome for most readers. The Annals stand as a master class in how power rots, told by a master.
tacitus-germania-agricola-church-brodrib:
Church and Brodribb translated two short Tacitus works together: the Germania and the Agricola. The Germania describes the tribes beyond Rome's Rhine frontier in 98 AD. The Agricola honors the author's father-in-law, a general in Britain.

Tacitus praises German freedom and simple ways to shame soft Rome. His tribal notes are the first ethnography of those peoples. Agricola's life shows conquest, rule, and recall by a jealous emperor. Both pieces are short and dense with insight. Together they form a classic pair: one on a foreign world, one on a good man serving bad times.
